UATU uses cross-portrayal archetype *gestalt* as background while compiling **separate, continuity-bounded variant profiles**. It creates temporary performance echoes, voice and visual briefs and a **versioned CastManifest**.\n5. Nerd Court receives the evidence and cast, conducts structured prosecution/defense, performs character-specific dialogue and witnesses, produces a cited verdict and permits an earned comedic or dramatic finisher.\n6. A production pipeline storyboards, records/synthesizes approved voices, animates shots, mixes, renders, encodes and checks a real video master.\n7. Job services keep the viewer informed, manage costs, persist published assets and optionally preserve an exact echo snapshot for a sequel. The video is playable via browser, phone or television app.\n\n## Proposed single-repo layout\n\n```text\nnerd-court/\n  architecture/knowledge-graph/      # current source-backed architecture records\n  architecture/contracts/            # versioned JSON interfaces (first migration unit)\n  apps/\n    web/                             # grievance, jobs, episode archive, player [PLANNED]\n    tv/                              # streaming-platform client [PLANNED]\n    ios-legacy/                      # move existing Swift code only after audit [PLANNED]\n  services/\n    identity/                        # classify and resolve actor / portrayal / variant [PLANNED]\n    canon-evidence/                  # claim provenance, tiered canon, conflicts [PLANNED]\n    uatu-casting/                    # variant psychology, ephemeral echoes, cast [PLANNED]\n    courtroom/                       # adversarial trial, judge and finisher rules [PLANNED]\n    showrunner/                       # scenes, timing, boards [PLANNED]\n    media-render/                     # animation, sound, encoding, QC [PLANNED]\n    jobs/                            # retries, idempotency, visibility [PLANNED]\n  packages/\n    contracts/                       # generated language bindings after schema review [PLANNED]\n    shared-tests/                     # source-backed fixtures, no cross-variant leakage [PLANNED]\n  infra/                              # deploy, access, secrets and storage policy [PLANNED]\n  docs/                               # operational how-to and design decisions [PLANNED]\n  Sources/, Tests/, convex/           # EXISTING Swift/Convex code, untouched on feature branch\n```\n\nThe layout is **a target**, not a claim that these directories or components exist today. Do not migrate by mass-copying the old repos; use pinned-source references until a candidate module has a passing characterization test and known license.\n\n## Identity contract\n\nThe identity hierarchy is `Archetype -> Variant -> EpisodeEcho`, with **parallel** entity types for performers and portrayals:\n\n- **Archetype:** an evidence-aware gestalt across portrayals; may contain conflicting versions, explicitly tagged.\n- **Variant:** fixed franchise, publisher, medium, universe, timeline, role, and era; exact source claims and relationship bounds.\n- **Performer:** real actor/person, not equivalent to an authored character; `portrays` is a typed edge, not an `is` edge.\n- **Portrayal:** an actor playing a role *in a named production* and, if applicable, within a specified fictional world.\n- **EpisodeEcho:** temporary performance state pinned to one variant or portrayal, one episode and one profile revision. The underlying canon never mutates when fiction happens in court.\n\nAs an example, **Robert Downey Jr., MCU Tony Stark, Downey's Lewis Strauss portrayal, Downey's Charlie Chaplin portrayal, and a specifically chosen Doctor Doom portrayal are five distinct records** even if jokes intentionally connect them. Do not assume Doom is MCU Stark in disguise just because the performer overlaps.\n\n## Data contracts to implement first\n\n- `Grievance`: the allegation, named entities, user constraints, user-entered continuity hints and submission identifier.\n- `EntityResolution`: entity kind, canonical ID, portrayal/actor mapping, evidence and ambiguity score.\n- `VariantProfile`: locked variant keys, citations, observed traits, modeled psychology and inferred claims clearly separated.\n- `CastManifest`: fixed episode ID, source/profile/voice/visual versions, roles, character-echo references, witnesses and provenance.\n- `EvidenceLedger`: citation anchors, direct source material, strength and contradiction handling.\n- `EpisodeJob`: explicit state transitions, inputs/outputs, failure, retries, cost, timing, artifact verification.\n- `EpisodeArtifact`: decodable video renditions, synchronized audio, captions, media hashes, review status and publication URI.\n\n## Boundaries that must not collapse\n\n| Boundary | Contract |\n|---|---|\n| Archetype vs variant | Gesture toward archetype for interpretation; do not import unrelated history or speech |\n| Variant vs performer | Link with `portrays`; never unify identities |\n| Research vs performance | Fact selection and uncertainty completed before actors begin improvising |\n| Episode improvisation vs source canon | Show-only events are in episode history, not canonical evidence |\n| Runtime echo vs durable profile | Echo lives for a job; serialize only if reuse approved |\n| Psychological inference vs observable canon | Mark estimates/hypotheses separately from cited actions |\n| Sound/animation playback vs video file | A scene executing in SpriteKit is not proof of encoded streaming media |\n| Completion flag vs acceptance | `SUCCESS` requires verified playable A/V output, not just a scripted transcript |\n\n## Build order\n\n**Phase A (current):** pin repos, construct knowledge graph and an explicit source/destination ledger, identify licensing and security exclusions.  \n**Phase B:** define versioned contracts; implement and test classification, continuity resolution and source ledger on a curated cross-franchise fixture set.  \n**Phase C:** integrate UATU deep assessment and a variant-exclusive compiler; test identity drift and echo lifecycle under restarts and crossover stimuli.  \n**Phase D:** integrate court debate, an evidence-backed judge, scene plans, staff/guest roles and finisher choreography; validate a complete **text-and-shot-plan trial**.  \n**Phase E:** implement actual animation, voice approvals, mixing, render/encode, captions and media validation; prove one complete A/V episode before scaling.  \n**Phase F:** add web + TV distribution, durable jobs, budgets, caching, observability, live capacity and measured long-episode turnaround.\n\nEach phase has its own acceptance tests; no phase is declared complete merely because a file or API route exists.\n\n## Graph-first development rule\n\nWhen a new module is merged:\n1. Add its source/provenance and destination owner node.\n2. Add observed import/call/data-flow edges after reviewing the actual code.\n3. Add a corresponding executable test and runtime status.\n4. Resolve discrepancies between aspirational README claims and implementation evidence.\n5. Maintain pinning and ensure no secret, licensed binary, or unwanted memory scope travels between repos.\n","message":"architecture: document UNIFIED-ARCHITECTURE.md mapping and migration gates"}}

import copy
import json
import tempfile
import unittest
from pathlib import Path

from validate_graph import validate_package, GraphError


class ValidatePackageTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.workspace = tempfile.TemporaryDirectory()
        self.root = Path(self.workspace.name)
        (self.root / 'sources').mkdir()
        (self.root / 'file-graphs').mkdir()
        self.semantic = {
            'schema': 'nerd-court-knowledge-graph/v1',
            'source_pins': [{'repository': 'oldmangrizzz/demo', 'commit': 'a' * 40}],
            'stats': {'nodes': 3, 'edges': 2},
            'nodes': [
                {'id': 'repo:demo', 'kind': 'repository', 'status': 'repository-indexed'},
                {'id': 'mod:reader', 'kind': 'module', 'repository': 'oldmangrizzz/demo', 'path': 'src/reader.py', 'status': 'file-present-not-runtime-verified'},
                {'id': 'target:ready', 'kind': 'target', 'status': 'planned'},
            ],
            'edges': [
                {'from': 'repo:demo', 'to': 'mod:reader', 'relation': 'contains'},
                {'from': 'mod:reader', 'to': 'target:ready', 'relation': 'candidate-for'},
            ],
        }
        self.inventory = {
            'schema': 'nerd-court-source-inventory/v1',
            'repository': 'oldmangrizzz/demo',
            'branch': 'main',
            'commit': 'a' * 40,
            'files': [{'path': 'src/reader.py', 'sha': 'b' * 40, 'bytes': 123}],
        }
        self.filegraph = {
            'schema': 'nerd-court-source-file-graph/v1',
            'source_repository': 'oldmangrizzz/demo',
            'source_commit': 'a' * 40,
            'counts': {'files': 1, 'folders': 1, 'nodes': 3, 'edges': 2},
            'nodes': [
                {'id': 'repo:demo', 'type': 'repository'},
                {'id': 'dir:demo:src', 'type': 'directory'},
                {'id': 'file:demo:src/reader.py', 'type': 'file', 'path': 'src/reader.py', 'sha': 'b' * 40},
            ],
            'edges': [
                {'from': 'repo:demo', 'to': 'dir:demo:src', 'type': 'contains'},
                {'from': 'dir:demo:src', 'to': 'file:demo:src/reader.py', 'type': 'contains'},
            ],
        }
        self.bridge = {
            'schema': 'nerd-court-semantic-file-bridge/v1',
            'edges': [{'from': 'mod:reader', 'to': 'file:demo:src/reader.py', 'relation': 'backed-by-source-file'}],
        }
        self.write_all()

    def tearDown(self):
        self.workspace.cleanup()

    def put(self, path, obj):
        (self.root / path).write_text(json.dumps(obj), encoding='utf-8')

    def write_all(self):
        self.put('semantic-graph.v1.json', self.semantic)
        self.put('semantic-file-bridges.v1.json', self.bridge)
        self.put('sources/demo.inventory.json', self.inventory)
        self.put('file-graphs/demo.graph.json', self.filegraph)

    def test_valid_package_has_fully_linked_source_evidence(self):
        report = validate_package(self.root)
        self.assertEqual(report['status'], 'passed')
        self.assertEqual(report['source_files'], 1)
        self.assertEqual(report['unique_nodes'], 5)
        self.assertEqual(report['total_edges'], 5)
        self.assertEqual(report['semantic_source_bridges'], 1)

    def test_rejects_dangling_semantic_reference(self):
        self.semantic['edges'][1]['to'] = 'target:not-a-node'
        self.write_all()
        with self.assertRaises(GraphError):
            validate_package(self.root)

    def test_rejects_wrong_pinned_file_hash(self):
        self.filegraph['nodes'][2]['sha'] = 'c' * 40
        self.write_all()
        with self.assertRaises(GraphError):
            validate_package(self.root)

    def test_rejects_missing_source_bridge(self):
        self.bridge['edges'] = []
        self.write_all()
        with self.assertRaises(GraphError):
            validate_package(self.root)

    def test_rejects_multiple_parents_in_source_tree(self):
        self.filegraph['edges'].append({'from': 'repo:demo', 'to': 'file:demo:src/reader.py', 'type': 'contains'})
        self.filegraph['counts']['edges'] += 1
        self.write_all()
        with self.assertRaises(GraphError):
            validate_package(self.root)

    def test_rejects_target_misrepresented_as_runtime_verified(self):
        self.semantic['nodes'][2]['status'] = 'implemented'
        self.write_all()
        with self.assertRaises(GraphError):
            validate_package(self.root)


if __name__ == '__main__':
    unittest.main()

"""Validate the source-backed Nerd Court/UATU architecture graph package.

This validates metadata, references, snapshot integrity, and declared status only.
It does NOT run, verify, or audit the behavior of any original application.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
from collections import Counter
from pathlib import Path


class GraphError(ValueError):
    """The knowledge graph's recorded facts are internally inconsistent."""


def _read(path: Path) -> dict:
    try:
        data = json.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    except (FileNotFoundError, OSError, json.JSONDecodeError) as exc:
        raise GraphError(f"Cannot read graph JSON {path}: {exc}") from exc
    if not isinstance(data, dict):
        raise GraphError(f"Graph document must be an object: {path}")
    return data


def _unique_ids(nodes: list, label: str) -> set[str]:
    identifiers = [node.get("id") for node in nodes]
    if any(not isinstance(item, str) or not item for item in identifiers):
        raise GraphError(f"Empty or invalid node ID in {label}")
    if len(identifiers) != len(set(identifiers)):
        raise GraphError(f"Duplicate node ID in {label}")
    return set(identifiers)


def _check_edges(edges: list, ids: set[str], label: str) -> None:
    for edge in edges:
        if edge.get("from") not in ids or edge.get("to") not in ids:
            raise GraphError(f"Dangling edge in {label}: {edge}")


def validate_package(root: str | Path) -> dict:
    """Validate linked semantic graph and pinned source-tree graph artifacts.

    Returns machine-readable counts only when all checks succeed.
    """
    root = Path(root)
    semantic = _read(root / "semantic-graph.v1.json")
    bridges = _read(root / "semantic-file-bridges.v1.json")
    sem_nodes = semantic.get("nodes", [])
    sem_edges = semantic.get("edges", [])
    sem_ids = _unique_ids(sem_nodes, "semantic graph")
    _check_edges(sem_edges, sem_ids, "semantic graph")
    stats = semantic.get("stats", {})
    if stats.get("nodes") != len(sem_nodes) or stats.get("edges") != len(sem_edges):
        raise GraphError("Semantic graph declared totals do not match its contents")

    module_nodes = [node for node in sem_nodes if node.get("kind") == "module"]
    if any(n.get("status") != "file-present-not-runtime-verified" for n in module_nodes):
        raise GraphError("Source-present modules cannot be claimed runtime-verified")
    if any(n.get("status") != "planned" for n in sem_nodes if n.get("kind") in ("target", "test")):
        raise GraphError("Unimplemented target or acceptance test claimed as complete")

    pins = semantic.get("source_pins", [])
    pinned_by_repo = {pin.get("repository"): pin.get("commit") for pin in pins}
    if len(pinned_by_repo) != len(pins):
        raise GraphError("Duplicate repository pin")

    total_files = total_folders = total_tree_nodes = total_tree_edges = 0
    ids_all = set(sem_ids)
    actual_file_ids: set[str] = set()
    all_inventoried_files: dict[tuple[str, str], str] = {}
    seen_names: set[str] = set()

    for inventory_path in sorted((root / "sources").glob("*.inventory.json")):
        name = inventory_path.name.removesuffix(".inventory.json")
        if name in seen_names:
            raise GraphError(f"Repeated inventory for {name}")
        seen_names.add(name)
        inventory = _read(inventory_path)
        file_graph = _read(root / "file-graphs" / f"{name}.graph.json")
        repository = inventory.get("repository")
        snapshot_sha = inventory.get("commit")
        if pinned_by_repo.get(repository) != snapshot_sha:
            raise GraphError(f"Unpinned or conflicting source inventory: {name}")
        if file_graph.get("source_repository") != repository or file_graph.get("source_commit") != snapshot_sha:
            raise GraphError(f"File graph built from a different source snapshot: {name}")
        files = inventory.get("files", [])
        file_by_path = {entry.get("path"): entry.get("sha") for entry in files}
        if len(file_by_path) != len(files):
            raise GraphError(f"Repeated tracked path in inventory: {name}")
        file_nodes = file_graph.get("nodes", [])
        tree_edges = file_graph.get("edges", [])
        local_ids = _unique_ids(file_nodes, f"file graph {name}")
        root_id = f"repo:{name}"
        if root_id not in local_ids or root_id not in sem_ids:
            raise GraphError(f"Unlinked repository root: {name}")
        if root_id not in [n["id"] for n in file_nodes if n.get("type") == "repository"]:
            raise GraphError(f"Repository node has wrong type: {name}")
        _check_edges(tree_edges, local_ids, f"file graph {name}")
        if len(tree_edges) != len(file_nodes) - 1:
            raise GraphError(f"File graph is not a tree: {name}")
        incoming = Counter(e["to"] for e in tree_edges)
        if incoming[root_id] or any(incoming[nid] != 1 for nid in local_ids - {root_id}):
            raise GraphError(f"Source tree node has zero/multiple parents: {name}")
        if any(e.get("type") != "contains" for e in tree_edges):
            raise GraphError(f"Unexpected relationship in source tree: {name}")
        observed_files = [n for n in file_nodes if n.get("type") == "file"]
        observed_folders = [n for n in file_nodes if n.get("type") == "directory"]
        if len(observed_files) != len(files):
            raise GraphError(f"Missing/extra file node: {name}")
        for node in observed_files:
            expected_id = f"file:{name}:{node.get('path')}"
            if node["id"] != expected_id or file_by_path.get(node.get("path")) != node.get("sha"):
                raise GraphError(f"File path or git blob SHA mismatch: {name}/{node.get('path')}")
            actual_file_ids.add(node["id"])
        for path, sha in file_by_path.items():
            all_inventoried_files[(repository, path)] = sha
        count = file_graph.get("counts", {})
        if (count.get("files"), count.get("folders"), count.get("nodes"), count.get("edges")) != (
            len(observed_files), len(observed_folders), len(file_nodes), len(tree_edges)
        ):
            raise GraphError(f"File graph metadata counts incorrect: {name}")
        ids_all.update(local_ids)
        total_files += len(files)
        total_folders += len(observed_folders)
        total_tree_nodes += len(file_nodes)
        total_tree_edges += len(tree_edges)

    if set(pinned_by_repo) != {f"oldmangrizzz/{name}" for name in seen_names}:
        raise GraphError("Not every repository pin has exactly one inventory")

    bridge_edges = bridges.get("edges", [])
    _check_edges(bridge_edges, ids_all, "semantic-file bridges")
    by_module = Counter(e.get("from") for e in bridge_edges)
    if len(bridge_edges) != len(module_nodes) or any(by_module[node["id"]] != 1 for node in module_nodes):
        raise GraphError("Each reviewed source module needs exactly one source-file bridge")
    for e in bridge_edges:
        if e.get("relation") != "backed-by-source-file" or e.get("to") not in actual_file_ids:
            raise GraphError(f"Invalid source bridge: {e}")
    for node in module_nodes:
        full_repo, path = node.get("repository"), node.get("path")
        if (full_repo, path) not in all_inventoried_files:
            raise GraphError(f"Module points outside pinned sources: {node['id']}")
        name = full_repo.split("/")[-1]
        if f"file:{name}:{path}" not in {e["to"] for e in bridge_edges if e["from"] == node["id"]}:
            raise GraphError(f"Module-to-file bridge disagrees with exact source path: {node['id']}")

    return {
        "status": "passed", "scope": "metadata-integrity-only; no source code execution",
        "repositories": len(seen_names), "source_files": total_files,
        "folders": total_folders, "semantic_nodes": len(sem_nodes), "semantic_edges": len(sem_edges),
        "source_file_nodes": total_tree_nodes, "source_tree_edges": total_tree_edges,
        "semantic_source_bridges": len(bridge_edges), "unique_nodes": len(ids_all),
        "total_edges": len(sem_edges) + total_tree_edges + len(bridge_edges),
    }


def main() -> None:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("root", nargs="?", default=".", help="Knowledge graph root folder")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    try:
        result = validate_package(args.root)
    except GraphError as error:
        parser.exit(1, f"Graph validation FAILED: {error}\n")
    print(json.dumps(result, indent=2))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

The graph is now versioned and checkable, not just visual. {"videoId":"S8g5nwZN9as","url":"https://youtu.be/S8g5nwZN9as?is=dFnpcRJckIT3GplL","type":"auto","lang":"en-orig","text":"Welcome back to GitHub awesome. This is GitHub trending weekly number 56. 35 trending open- source projects on GitHub right now. Let's go. Caro gives your coding agents a terminal that remembers where you left them. Claude Code, Codeex, your dev server. Each gets its own session grouped by project. The sidebar shows which ones need your attention, and closing the window doesn't kill their work. You can even bring sessions from a remote machine into the same view. That's handy when your laptop isn't the one doing the heavy lifting. UB mode is Uncle Bob's agent skill for writing clean code built from a trimmed set of potatoes rules and paired with real measuring tools. It pushes your coding agent toward test-driven development and tests that check behavior, not implementation details. Each change has to pass hard limits. a complexity score under 10 and a duplication score under 0.8. Mutation testing then breaks the code on purpose to make sure the tests notice. Dossier is a self-hosted job search app that writes tailored resumes and cover letters from a single career profile. Paste in a job posting or search job boards and the AI pulls out the requirements and shows how well you match. Then it drafts your documents using only facts from your profile which you can refine in a chat and export as PDFs. It runs on a local model or a hosted API and your data lives in your own database. OXR is a document parsing model from Somark that turns PDFs and scan pages into markdown or JSON, keeping the layout coordinates for every block. It has 1.3 billion parameters and was trained from scratch. A separate layout model finds the blocks. Then OXR reads their content and puts them in order. It recognizes 13 kinds of elements from tables and formulas to chemical structures and code. Strata runs AI models on your own computer without making you piece together and set up yourself. Pick a model in the desktop app or launch one from the terminal and Strata helps get it running on your hardware. It works with supported Nvidia and AMD cards, Apple Silicon, and Intel Arc on Linux. You can also connect its local models to Claude Code, Codeex CLI, and other coding tools. Print my profile pick is a playful hardware project from Andrew Schmemellion. Star the repo and your GitHub profile picture gets printed on a receipt printer. A star sends a web hook through a Cloudflare tunnel to a small PHP script on a Raspberry Pi. The script grabs your avatar and name, places them inside a little frame, and prints the receipt on a printer. Each one gets pinned to a wall he calls the hall of frame. Motti puts your remote server tools in one native desktop app, so you don't have to jump between separate clients just to get work done. It combines SSH terminals, SFTP file transfers, port forwarding, and VNC or RDP sessions in the same window. There's also an AI assistant and MCP support. It's built in Go with the Viva UI framework without bundling a web view. Flare is Nvidia's local inference server for its newest GPUs like the DGX Spark built for long conversations and coding agents that call tools over and over. All the compiling and CUDA graph setup happens ahead of time in PyTorch and gets packaged up. Then a Rust runtime with no Python serves that package. So nothing has to compile once you start. Floor plan turns your codebase into an interactive map when you need to figure out how an app actually fits together. Ask Claude Code or Codeex to draw one and you can zoom from the big picture down to individual files and endpoints. It follows connections between front-end requests and backend routes, even across repos. You can also ask the map a question and get a smaller diagram of the pieces involved. Open Duet is Copilot Kit's open-source proactive agent that gets work done before you ask. Built on their OpenBot platform, it starts your day with a short brief of what changed and what needs a decision from you. It sorts your mail and calendar into what needs you now and what can wait. hand it a task and it keeps working on a computer of its own with a real browser and its own files. Cargle's calendar prototype gives you a working interface to study instead of another static dashboard mockup. You can drag events around the calendar, resize them, and switch between day, week, and month views. The time off page counts working days and previews the remaining balance. It's built with Nex.js JS and runs entirely in the browser, so the data stays in local storage and there's no backend. Zeroach toolkit is a free Python tool that checks your computer, your Android phone, or an iPhone backup for traces of known mercenary spyware like Pegasus, Predator, and Graphite. It only reads, never changes anything, and makes no requests while it scans. It compares what it finds against published indicators from security researchers. Bigga turns a flatpack furniture product name or article number into an animated 3D assembly guide drawn in the familiar black and white line art style. It's built with Nex.js and 3JS and a generator works out the steps for more than 1100 products on its own with no AI call needed. You can step through a guide by voice, print it, or ask a help chat to redraw a confusing step. Kinsaku is a local desktop search app for your files, documents, code, and images. It reads each file once and builds both a keyword index and a semantic one, so you can search by exact words or by meaning. It pulls text out of PDFs, office files, and code, and even reads text in screenshots with OCR. Results are ranked by relevance, similarity, how recent they are, and where they live. Bama, short for build any Mac app, is a set of agent skills for cloud code and codecs that takes a native Mac OS app from idea to working build in Swift and Swift UI. The agent turns your idea into user stories with acceptance criteria and groups them into milestones. Then it builds one story per commit, snapshots every screen in light and dark mode, and runs the tests. Hokum gives your Whan desktop a control center for notifications, sound, and Bluetooth. Notification cards slide in and rearrange themselves, while a tray panel puts volume, connected devices, and do not disturb close at hand. You can pair Bluetooth devices from the app and control notifications with keyboard shortcuts. It's written in Rust and works with compositors like Hyperland, Sway, and Neri. Devbox is Rudderstack's open- source coding agent that you run in your own cloud. Give it a task from the command line or from Linear and it plans the change, writes the code, runs the tests, and reviews its own diff. Then it opens a draft pull request for a person to merge. No code gets written until the plan passes review and CI failures and review comments go straight back to the running task. Duckpad is an open- source SQL workspace for building visual data pipelines powered by DuckDB and installed as a Python package. You connect sources, joins, and reusable parts into a pipeline or write SQL directly in the editor. Click any cell in a result and it traces back to the exact source values that produced it. Projects save to git so you can branch, compare changes, and review merges just like code. Pika H3 Flex is an openweight video model from PA Labs that generates video with matching stereo audio built as adapters on top of Miniaax's H3. You can start from a text prompt, a first frame, a last frame, both, or up to 12 reference images and clips. It renders 5 to 15sec videos at up to 768p across 11 aspect ratios in only six sampling steps. The analytics playbook is Atlan's open guide to building AI analytics agents that give the right business numbers. It walks through five phases with a check at the end of each one. You start by locking in a golden set of real questions from your analysts before building anything. Then you pull metric definitions out of your past SQL and dashboards and improve the agent by studying where it fails. Kinettoraphph is a programmatic video engine built for AI agents. You write videos in Typescript with Remotions API using CSS, SVG, canvas, and even webgl shaders. Instead of driving a hidden Chrome browser, it uses a Rust compositor on the GPU with Skia and FFmpeg, so there's no browser anywhere in the pipeline. Existing Remotion projects render asis, and it ships an MCP server, so an agent can drive it. ESP32 USB to AirPrint is firmware that turns an old USBon printer into a wireless one using a cheap ESP32S3 board. Plug the board into the printer's USB port. Connect it to your Wi-Fi and it speaks the printer's USB protocol for you. Then your iPhone and Mac can print over AirPrint, Android phones over Mopria, and Linux 2 with no drivers or apps. Survival LLM is a free AI assistant for emergency and survival questions that runs entirely on your own computer with no internet needed. It uses local models through Olama and answers from an offline library of medical, emergency, and how-to articles drawn from sources like Wikipedia, Medline Plus, the CDC, and FEMA. Every answer shows the articles it used, and the app checks that those really are the articles it opened. AIP phone turns an Apple Silicon Mac into a voice agent that can make and answer phone calls. Give it a task like asking a restaurant about a reservation and it returns a transcript when the call ends. Speech recognition and voice generation run locally and you can choose a local model for the conversation, too. Outgoing calls start with an AI disclosure and it currently handles one English call at a time. Lightost is a self-hosted social media scheduler that lets you prepare one post and send it to multiple accounts from a single dashboard. It supports platforms including Blue Sky, Mastadon, Instagram, and Telegram with posts you can publish immediately or schedule for later. It runs on Python and SQLite. And the creator says it's light enough to run on a Raspberry Pi 0. Glyph brings the look of nothing OS to a hyperland desktop with black backgrounds, dotted white text, and a splash of red. It's built with quick shell and includes a launcher, quick settings, screenshots, and a lock screen. The screen edges even light up for things like volume changes and notifications. If you like tweaking your Linux desktop, there's plenty here to take apart. Mini CPM OCR turns PDFs and document images into usable text, tables, and formulas, even when the pages are photographed or curved. The interesting part is its companion model, Jev, which scores individual regions of the result to help you find what needs a closer look. You can run the models locally and export parsed documents as markdown or JSON. Lever is GitHub's plugin of copilot skills for building feedback loops for coding agents. You define a metric, a way to measure it, and a bar for what counts as better. And the agent keeps iterating until it clears that bar. One command picks a playbook for briefing a task, delivering it, refactoring, or shephering a pull request through to merge. Autonomy levels from 0 to 5 decide how much the agent can do on its own. Dontello is a tiny Mac OS tool that automatically clicks don't allow on those find devices on your local network popups written in Swift with no dependencies. It runs quietly in the background and uses no CPU until a prompt shows up. When one does it checks the dialogue really is a local network request and that the app isn't on your allow list, then denies it. Video to game is a skill for coding agents like Claude Code and Codeex that turns a gameplay video into a playable browser game built with 3JS. The agent studies the clip frame by frame pulling out the look, the pallet, and the cuts. It writes a game spec, generates every asset through foul from images to 3D models and sound, and builds the whole game into one HTML file. Grimrompter is a set of threat modeling prompts for coding agents like Claude Code and Codeex from security expert Jim Manico. Link its skill into your agent and ask for a threat model quick or deep. The agent reads your code without changing anything and works through established frameworks like Stride and MITER attack. Every finding points to the exact file and line, and each proposed fix comes with a plan for checking it actually works. Skill diet is an agent skill that keeps your other agent skills lean, building on Matt PCO's writing for agents rules. It measures a skill, cuts what the model already knows, and rewrites the rest. Then it runs a before and after test, and only keeps the slimmer version if agents do at least as well. For skills that wrap a command line tool or an API, it also checks the instructions against the real tool and reads session logs to find the calls you use most. Agent Loop is a Go library for building AI agents without writing the tool calling loop from scratch. It sends requests to a model, runs the tools it asks for, and feeds the results back until there's an answer. You can set budgets, add approval hooks, and inspect a trace of each run. It also includes search and coding agents as examples so you can see how the pieces fit together. Filmic is a plugin that adds real-time film emulation to Unreal Engine 5. Drop one actor into your level. Pick a look and it runs a whole chain of effects. Film color, animated grain, hellation around bright lights, bloom, and lens artifacts. A single slider blends between Unreal's own output and the film look. Every one of its nearly 200 settings can be animated in sequencer or driven from blueprints. English RS is a Rust project that checks English grammar the way the compiler checks code. Write a sentence inside its macro and Rust's type system catches mistakes like a singular subject with a plural verb or the wrong article. It even treats pronouns as borrows of the nouns they refer to. probably with a lot of help from AI, and it works. But ask \"what happens when someone checks out?\" or \"what breaks if I change this?\" and the honest answer is *no idea*.\n\nFloorplan gives you the diagram nobody drew. Ask Claude Code or Codex for a floorplan and a few minutes later you have a map you can explore, ask questions on, and keep up to date as you work.\n\n- **For builders:** understand the app you made, in your own words, without reading the code.\n- **For teams:** onboard someone in minutes, from the big picture down to the exact file.\n- **For working with AI:** after every change Claude or Codex makes, see exactly which parts it touched and why.\n\n## Features\n\n<table>\n<tr>\n<td width=\"50%\" valign=\"top\">\n\n**🗺️ A map at every zoom**<br>\nStart with the whole app, then double-click into a part, a group of files, a file, and its endpoints. Each view shows what it's used by and what it uses.\n\n</td>\n<td width=\"50%\" valign=\"top\">\n\n**💬 Plain English everywhere**<br>\n\"Takes card payments at checkout\", not \"Stripe API wrapper\". Technical terms are explained on hover, and one switch shows the developer view.\n\n</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td valign=\"top\">\n\n**🔌 Real connections, across repos**<br>\nIt follows imports, and matches each web request in your frontend to the server endpoint that answers it, even across separate repos.\n\n</td>\n<td valign=\"top\">\n\n**🖥️ Start from a screen**<br>\nPick a page you know and see everything behind it: its parts, the requests it makes, the server code, the data, and outside services.\n\n</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td valign=\"top\">\n\n**🧭 Ask the map**<br>\n\"How does a refund reach the customer's card?\" comes back as an answer plus a mini-map of just the pieces involved, with a step-by-step walkthrough.\n\n</td>\n<td valign=\"top\">\n\n**🩺 Health check**<br>\nFinds passwords in code, endpoints anyone can use without signing in, unused files and files too big to edit safely. Each comes with a ready-to-paste fix.\n\n</td>\n</tr>\n<tr>\n<td valign=\"top\">\n\n**🟢 Recent work**<br>\nThe cards your AI just changed light up green, each with a note on how the change serves what you asked for.\n\n</td>\n<td valign=\"top\">\n\n**⚡ Stays current, stays yours**<br>\nUpdates re-read only what changed, and an open map reloads itself. Everything runs on your machine, and nothing is committed to git.\n\n</td>\n</tr>\n</table>\n\nPlus guided **flows** you can request in plain words, a one-minute **Start here** tour, search, keyboard shortcuts, and right-click actions on every card.\n\n### Also: blueprints, for apps you haven't built yet\n\nFloorplan is made for mapping code you already have. It can also start from a PRD, a spec or a description of something you want to build, and draw a **blueprint**: the same kind of map, showing every part, file, endpoint and screen you'd need and how they'd fit together. Cards are dashed to show it's a plan. Instead of a Health check you get a review of what the plan still leaves open, each part has a ready request to build it, and you can reshape the plan from the map (\"also plan out refunds\"). Once the code exists, the blueprint becomes a map of the real thing. See [Plan something you haven't built yet](docs/getting-started.md#plan-something-you-havent-built-yet).\n\n## See it in action\n\nWant to click around yourself? Floorplan runs on the plan you already have, with no API keys.\n\n### Claude Code\n\nIn the desktop app's Code tab or the CLI:\n\n```bash\nclaude plugin marketplace add haydenschmitty/floorplan\nclaude plugin install floorplan@floorplan\n```\n\nStart a new session and it's ready. Installing the Claude Code CLI is recommended even if you use the desktop app, because it lets the map's Ask bar read your real code. More in [Getting started](docs/getting-started.md).\n\n### Codex\n\nSigned in with ChatGPT. No terminal needed:\n\n1. In the Codex app, open **Plugins** and choose **Add a marketplace**.\n2. For **Source**, enter `haydenschmitty/floorplan` and click **Add marketplace**.\n3. Find **Floorplan** and click **+** to install it.\n\nOr, from a terminal:\n\n```bash\ncodex plugin marketplace add haydenschmitty/floorplan\ncodex plugin add floorplan@floorplan\n```\n\nStart a new chat and ask for a floorplan, or type `$floorplan`. The map's Ask bar runs on your own Codex sign-in, with no API key. More in [Floorplan in Codex](docs/codex.md).\n\n## Quick start\n\n1. Open your project in Claude Code or Codex. For a frontend and backend in separate repos, open the folder that holds both.\n2. Ask:\n   > Make me a floorplan of this app.\n\n   (In Codex you can also type `$floorplan`.)\n3. Explore. The map opens on its own, starting with a short tour.\n\nWhen you've done more work, ask:\n\n> Update the floorplan.\n\nOnly what changed is re-read, and what you just worked on lights up under **Recent work**.\n\n**No code yet?** Floorplan can plan an app from a PRD or spec instead. Share the document and ask:\n\n> Here's my PRD. Make me a floorplan of what we'd need to build.\n\nYou get a [blueprint](#also-blueprints-for-apps-you-havent-built-yet) of the planned system, clearly marked as a plan.\n\n### Things to try\n\n| Ask Claude Code or Codex | Ask the map |\n|---|---|\n| \"Make me a floorplan of this app\" | \"What happens when someone places an order?\" |\n| \"Update the floorplan\" | \"Where do we talk to Stripe?\" |\n| \"Fix the important issues from the floorplan's Health check\" | \"If I change the users table, what breaks?\" |\n| \"Add a flow showing how a new user signs up\" | \"Which files handle login?\" |\n| \"Rewrite the floorplan for developers\" | \"What did we change for refunds?\" |\n\n## How it works\n\n```mermaid\nflowchart LR\n    code[\"Your codebase<br/>one repo or several\"] --> scan[\"Scan<br/>files, imports, routes, requests\"]\n    scan --> agent[\"Claude or Codex<br/>names the parts, describes every file\"]\n    agent --> build[\"Build<br/>map, health, screens, recent work\"]\n    build --> map[\"floorplan/index.html<br/>opens in your browser\"]\n    map -. \"update the floorplan\" .-> scan\n```\n\nScripts do the mechanical work: finding repos, parsing code in a dozen languages, matching web requests to endpoints, laying out the map. They're plain Node with no dependencies. Claude or Codex does the part only a reader can: deciding what the parts of your app *are*, and saying so plainly. Details in [How it works](docs/how-it-works.md).\n\n**Languages:** TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Go, Rust, Java, Kotlin, Scala, plus Vue, Svelte and Astro files, with lighter support for others.<br>\n**Endpoints:** Express, Koa, Hono, Next.js, Firebase Cloud Functions, Flask, FastAPI, Django, Go's net/http, Gin, Echo and chi, Actix, Axum, Spring.<br>\n**Screens:** Next.js, React Router, Vue, SvelteKit, Remix, Nuxt, Astro, Expo, Angular, TanStack.\n\n## What it adds to your project\n\nA `floorplan/` folder holding the map. In Claude Code it also adds a short section to `CLAUDE.local.md` so future sessions know the map is there. **Neither is committed:** the folder ignores itself in git, and `CLAUDE.local.md` goes in your clone's private ignore list. In Codex, only the `floorplan/` folder is added. Your `.gitignore` and other tracked files are never touched. See [What's in your project](docs/project-files.md).\n\n## Privacy\n\n- The scan, the map and its small local server all run on your computer. The server only accepts connections from your own machine.\n- No dependencies or install scripts, and the map works offline: its layout engine and fonts are built in.\n- Questions on the map go to your own account, through the Claude Code CLI or Codex, which can read your code but not change it.\n- The Health check never stores or shows secret values, only where they are.\n- No analytics or tracking. The map may ask once whether you'd like an email when Floorplan Cloud launches. Nothing is sent unless you sign up, and then only your email and \"just me\" or \"with my team\".\n\nMore in [Privacy and security](docs/privacy-and-security.md).\n\n## Documentation\n\n| | |\n|---|---|\n| [Getting started](docs/getting-started.md) | Install, first map, updating, planning from a PRD, removing |\n| [Floorplan in Codex](docs/codex.md) | Installing and using it in Codex |\n| [Using the map](docs/using-the-map.md) | Every button, view, shortcut and menu |\n| [How it works](docs/how-it-works.md) | The pipeline, connection matching, refreshes |\n| [What's in your project](docs/project-files.md) | Every file Floorplan creates, and how to edit it |\n| [Privacy and security](docs/privacy-and-security.md) | What runs where, and what leaves your machine |\n| [Troubleshooting](docs/troubleshooting.md) | Common problems and fixes |\n| [Developing Floorplan](docs/development.md) | Repo layout, local installs, releases |\n\n## FAQ\n\n<details>\n<summary><b>Does my code leave my computer?</b></summary>\n\nOnly the way Claude Code and Codex always work: the AI reads the files it needs to describe your app, through your own account. The map itself is a local file and its server only listens on your machine. If you choose to open the map in the Claude app instead, Claude uploads the map (names, descriptions and structure, not your source code) to your private claude.ai account, and asks first. The one thing Floorplan itself ever sends is your email, and only if you sign up for the [Floorplan Cloud waitlist](docs/privacy-and-security.md#floorplan-cloud-waitlist).\n</details>\n\n<details>\n<summary><b>How long does it take, and what does it cost?</b></summary>\n\nA first map takes a few minutes for a small app and longer for a big one, because every file and endpoint gets described. It uses your Claude or ChatGPT plan like any other task. Big projects are split across parallel helpers. Updates re-read only what changed, so they're quick and cheap.\n</details>\n\n<details>\n<summary><b>Do I need a CLI for the Ask bar?</b></summary>\n\nNo. The map works without one. showcases](docs/showcases.md)\n\nThese are creative showcases, not release-validation renders or throughput benchmarks. Exact reproduction with the released package is not guaranteed.\n\n## System overview\n\nPika H3 Flex is one video-and-audio model family with two task adapters: FL2VA for text and endpoint-frame conditioning, and Ref2VA for multimodal references. It builds on [MiniMax-H3](https://huggingface.co/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-H3) and generates video with synchronized stereo audio in six sampling steps.\n\nThe inference pipeline encodes the prompt and input media, generates video and audio latents with the selected Pika H3 Flex adapter, then decodes and combines them into an MP4. The package downloads the pinned base components and adapter automatically. Use the [prompt guide](docs/prompt-guidance.md) to describe scenes, motion, dialogue, ambience and music; optional [prompt enhancement](https://dev.pika.art/models/pika/pika-h3-flex/prompt-rewriter) is available through the Pika API.\n\n### Input and output specifications\n\n| Category                 | Specification                                                                                                     |\n| ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |\n| Input modalities         | Text; first/last images; image, video and audio references, depending on the selected mode                        |\n| Native output resolution | 480p / 768p across all 11 supported aspect ratios; exact pixel dimensions follow the selected aspect-ratio bucket |\n| Output duration          | Requested integer durations of 5–15 seconds; actual length follows the model frame grid                          |\n| Output aspect ratios     | 21:9, 16:9, 3:2, 4:3, 5:4, 1:1, 4:5, 3:4, 2:3, 9:16, 9:21; dimensions use the packaged resolution buckets         |\n| Output frame rate        | 24 fps                                                                                                            |\n| Output audio             | 32 kHz stereo, mixed into the generated video                                                                     |\n| Output files             | MP4 with H.264 video and AAC audio, plus JSON generation metadata                                                 |\n| Prompt input             | Text or a UTF-8 prompt file; 1–8,000 characters                                                                  |\n| Sampling                 | Six generator evaluations using the released adapter's sampling schedule                                          |\n\nDurations are rounded up to the supported frame grid: a 5-second request produces 124 frames (about 5.17 seconds), and a 15-second request produces 362 frames (about 15.08 seconds). Native resolution and aspect ratio jointly determine the actual canvas dimensions.\n\n### Generation modes and reference limits\n\n| Mode                              | Inputs                                                                      | Adapter / CLI task  |\n| --------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------- |\n| Text to video and audio           | Prompt, without input media                                                 | FL2VA / `t2va`    |\n| First-frame conditioning          | Prompt and one opening frame                                                | FL2VA / `i2va`    |\n| Last-frame conditioning           | Prompt and one ending frame                                                 | FL2VA / `l2va`    |\n| First-and-last-frame conditioning | Prompt and both endpoint frames                                             | FL2VA / `fl2va`   |\n| Multimodal references             | Prompt and ordered image/video references, optionally with audio references | Ref2VA / `ref2va` |\n\nRef2VA accepts up to **9 images, 3 videos and 3 standalone audio clips**, with **12 reference files total**. At least one image or video is required. Each video or standalone audio clip must be **2–15 seconds**; combined video duration and combined standalone-audio duration must each be at most **15 seconds**. A video's embedded soundtrack stays with that video and does not count as an additional standalone audio file.\n\nThese are accepted input limits, not a guarantee that every maximum-size combination fits GPU memory. The package runs one request on one GPU, with optional CPU offload. See [hardware requirements and tested configurations](docs/hardware.md) for representative H100 results and memory guidance.\n\n## Pika API extensions\n\nExtend your generation workflow with Pika’s hosted endpoints:\n\n| Feature                 | Support                                            | Endpoint                                                                           |\n| ----------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |\n| Higher-resolution video | Generate 1080p, 2K and 4K video from a draft video | [Draft to video](https://dev.pika.art/models/pika/pika-h3-flex/draft-to-video)      |\n| Audio stems             | Obtain separate audio stems                        | [Audio stems](https://dev.pika.art/models/pika/pika-h3-flex/audio-stems)            |\n| Prompt enhancement      | Enhance generation prompts                         | [Prompt enhancement](https://dev.pika.art/models/pika/pika-h3-flex/prompt-rewriter) |\n\nThese optional hosted services are separate from the downloadable adapters and local inference package. The specifications above describe local model inference; see each endpoint’s documentation for its API capabilities and usage.\n\n## Install\n\nThe command and Python distribution are named `pika-h3-pro`.\n\nClone the repository, then enter its directory:\n\n```bash\ngit clone https://github.com/Pika-Labs/Pika-H3-Flex.git\ncd Pika-H3-Flex\n```\n\nFor pip installation, install system `git`, `patch`, `ffmpeg` and a C compiler with development headers first (for example, `build-essential` on Debian/Ubuntu). Triton needs the compiler at runtime. Docker and Conda recipes supply these prerequisites.\n\nUse Python 3.12, an NVIDIA GPU and a compatible driver. Representative cases are tested on one H100 80GB per request; H200 and B300 remain untested. Longer clips and large reference sets can exceed GPU memory. Downloading both tasks acquired approximately 210 GB of base files plus 5.5 GB of adapters; allow additional space for dependencies and download staging. See [tested cases and memory measurements](docs/hardware.md).\n\n**GPU selection:** the current package runs one request on one GPU. The examples expose a single GPU with `--gpus 'device=0'`; exposing eight GPUs does not shard or accelerate a request. Multiple idle GPUs can run independent processes. Start qualification at 480p / 5 seconds. Multi-GPU inference within one request is not implemented in this package.\n\n```bash\npython -m pip install -r requirements.txt\npython tools/apply_diffusers_patches.py\npython -m pip install --no-deps -e .\npika-h3-pro --help\n```\n\nAlternatively, create the Conda environment, then install the package:\n\n```bash\nconda env create -f environment.yml\nconda activate pika-h3-pro\npython tools/apply_diffusers_patches.py\npython -m pip install --no-deps -e .\n```\n\nFor Docker:\n\n```bash\ndocker build -t pika-h3-pro .\ndocker run --rm --gpus 'device=0' pika-h3-pro --help\n```\n\nThe three recipes share `requirements.txt`. [L2]   "content": "# Filmimic\n\n**Real-time film emulation for Unreal Engine. Drop in an Actor, pick a look, then make it yours.**\n\n[中文说明](README.zh-CN.md) · [Full user guide / 完整使用指南](docs/guide.zh-CN.md) · [Build and validation](docs/validation.md) · [License scope](docs/third-party-notices.md)\n\n![ArchVis interior rendered in Unreal Engine with Filmimic Kodak Portra 400](docs/images/portra.png)\n\nFilmimic brings film color, animated grain, halation, bloom, lens artifacts and framing controls into one Unreal post-process workflow. It includes **21 looks**, **197 effect parameters**, reusable preset assets, Blueprint controls and four quality tiers.\n\nThe initial public source snapshot is **1.0.0**. The tested baseline is **Unreal Engine 5.8.3 / Windows / DX12 / SM6**. This repository contains plugin sources and the assets needed by those sources; it does not contain Unreal Engine, compiled plugin binaries, private project maps or build caches.\n\n## See the difference\n\nSame scene, camera and lighting; different preset selections. These are actual Unreal `SceneCapture2D` renders, not externally applied filters or generated concept art.\n\n| Native Unreal | Kodak Portra 400 |\n| :---: | :---: |\n| ![Native Unreal output](docs/images/native.png) | ![Kodak Portra 400 preset](docs/images/portra.png) |\n\n| Kodak Gold 200 | Red Velvet | Cinematica |\n| :---: | :---: | :---: |\n| ![Kodak Gold 200 preset](docs/images/gold.png) | ![Red Velvet preset](docs/images/velvet.png) | ![Cinematica preset](docs/images/cinematica.png) |\n\nThe showcase uses the project's **ArchVis sample interior**, with its original lights, Lumen GI/reflections and temporal anti-aliasing requested. Each 2560×1440 image is captured after 100 real Editor warm-up frames. [Capture settings and reproduction instructions](docs/screenshots.md) document the camera and required sample content. The map and its assets are not bundled with the plugin. Preset names identify artistic looks, not a guarantee of a physical film stock's response or an endorsement by a film manufacturer.\n\n## What you can control\n\n| Area | Included controls |\n| --- | --- |\n| Film emulation | 14 film branches plus None, white balance, highlight/shadow tone, saturation, clarity and sharpness |\n| Grain | Quick size/roughness choices or advanced ISO, size, roughness and softness; optional animation |\n| Lens effects | Vignette, bloom, glints, halation, soft glow, ghosts, flare streaks, dispersion, fringing and lens dirt |\n| Grading | Flicker, split toning, punchiness, color adjustments and stylized 2D blur |\n| Overlays | Composition grids, borders, film sprockets and text watermarks |\n| Workflow | Shared or per-Actor settings, parameter resets, name-based Blueprint access and save-your-own presets |\n\nParameters are grouped in Details. Controls that do not affect the current branch are greyed out. Hover a label for a Chinese explanation, units and its parameter identifier; angle controls display degrees.\n\n## Install from source\n\n1. Install UE 5.8.3 and the C++ toolchain supported by that engine version.\n2. With your Editor closed, clone the repository into your project's plugin folder:\n\n   ```powershell\n   git clone https://github.com/DreamyLab30/Filmimic.git .\\Plugins\\Filmimic\n   ```\n\n3. Build your project's **Editor** target. A Blueprint-only project may need a C++ module or a locally built plugin package before it can load a source plugin.\n4. Open the project, enable **Filmimic** under **Edit → Plugins**, then restart the Editor. The shader module loads at engine startup.\n5. Add **FilmimicActor** to your level. In Details, choose **Preset**. Enable **Show Plugin Content** in the Content Browser to browse `/Filmimic` assets.\n\nTo build a distributable plugin locally, use the supplied wrapper with your own engine location and a **new output directory outside the repository**:\n\n```powershell\n.\\scripts\\build.ps1 -EngineRoot $env:UE_ROOT -OutputDirectory $env:FILMIMIC_PACKAGE_DIR\n```\n\n`UE_ROOT` is the folder containing the engine's `Engine` directory. BuildPlugin compiling successfully does not verify a cooked game; that is a separate test.\n\n## Make a look in five steps\n\n1. Select a preset such as **Kodak Portra 400**, **Cinematica** or **Red Velvet**.\n2. Click **Edit on this actor** to copy the shared preset into this Actor's local settings.\n3. Adjust exposure and film color first, then grain and lens effects. Use the group checkboxes to isolate an effect.\n4. Enter a name in **Save as Preset**, then click **Save Preset**. It writes a new asset under `/Game/FilmimicPresets`, selects it immediately and adds it to the preset dropdown. Existing names require overwrite confirmation.\n5. Save the level to retain the Actor's reference to the new preset.\n\n**Shared settings** follow the preset asset, including later edits to it. **Local settings** affect just this Actor. Selecting another preset in local mode replaces the local values; save a useful look before switching. Presets store effect settings and resource bindings, not an Actor's position, area radius or `Weight`.\n\n## The three controls worth learning first\n\n| Control | Meaning |\n| --- | --- |\n| **Enabled** | Off restores the native UE path for this Actor. |\n| **Weight** | Blend between native Unreal output (`0`) and Filmimic (`1`). Use this for fades and before/after comparisons. |\n| **Intensity** | Strength inside the Filmimic effect chain. At `0`, the AgX display transform remains; this is different from disabling Filmimic. |\n\n**Use Engine Exposure** is on by default. **Exposure EV** adds stops before the effect chain. The quick **Cinematic** quality tier is the default; **Reference** retains the highest-precision path and is much more expensive.\n\n## Blueprints, Sequencer and regions\n\nGet the Actor's `Filmimic` component and call:\n\n```text\nSetMenuParameterByName(\n    Name = \"Film Emulation / Film Type / Film Type\",\n    Option = \"VELVET / Vivid\")\n\nSetParameterByName(\n    Name = \"Lens Effects / Halation / Strength\",\n    Value = 0.2)\n\nFadeWeight(TargetWeight = 0, DurationSeconds = 1.5)\nBlendToPreset(TargetPreset, DurationSeconds = 2.0)\n```\n\n`GetAnimatableParameterNames` lists valid names; `GetParameterDescription` returns their explanations. `ApplyPreset` follows a shared asset; `LoadPresetAsLocal` copies it into this Actor. Transitions interpolate continuous controls; menu and switch choices change at the midpoint.\n\nThe **Animated Controls A–D** slots expose four selected numeric parameters to Sequencer. `Weight`, `Intensity` and `Exposure EV` also support keyframes. Clear a slot to stop its value overriding the ordinary parameter.\n\nLeave **Unbound** on for a world-wide look. Turn it off to use **Radius** and **Blend Distance** around the Actor. The highest-priority enabled candidate owns the view and fades toward native Unreal output; overlapping Filmimic Actors do not perform arbitrary multi-look blending.\n\n## Built-in looks\n\nDefault · Astra 1996 · Cinematica · Eternally Expired · Golden Chrome · Kodak 1971 · Kodak Ektra · Kodak Gold 200 · Kodak Portra 160 · Kodak Portra 400 · Kodak Portra Pro · Nostalgic Breeze · Pacifica · Red Velvet · SoCal · Sprint Clarity · Stonewall · Summer of 76 · Superia · Victoria · Yeast Lords\n\n`FilmimicActor.GetAvailablePresets()` returns these 21 assets. `FilmimicPresetCatalog.FindPresetByName()` resolves a display name. Saved user presets appear after the bundled looks in the editor dropdown.\n\n## Performance and support boundaries\n\nHistorical development measurements on an RTX 4090, Default preset, isolated SceneCapture and Insights GPU timing:\n\n| Output | Cinematic | Balanced | Performance | Reference |\n| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |\n| 1920×1080 | 1.98 ms | 1.85 ms | 1.65 ms | 28.7 ms |\n| 3840×2160 | 9.8 ms | — | 3.5 ms | — |\n\nThese are plugin GPU timings from the development harness, not complete game-frame times or a fresh cross-hardware benchmark. At high resolution, Performance reduces the grain domain and may soften/ring high-contrast edges. Profile your own scene with `stat gpu`. [Validation notes](docs/validation.md) distinguish historical evidence from this repository's fresh checks.\n\n- Editor viewport and PIE were exercised during development. The standalone source build and the ArchVis captures were verified for this public snapshot.\n- Cooked-game execution, other engine versions/platforms and Movie Render Queue are not yet verified.\n- HDR output encoding has numerical checks; a physical HDR display has not been validated. VR is experimental and disabled by default.\n- SceneCapture participation is opt-in via **Allow Scene Capture**. Reflection and planar-reflection captures are excluded.\n- At `Weight = 1`, Filmimic replaces the tonemapper. UE tonemapper color grading/LUTs therefore do not compose as ordinary additional grading; use Filmimic controls or native-image blending deliberately.\n- The plugin's **Stylized 2D Blur** is a whole-image effect. It does not replace velocity-based motion blur.\n\n## Contribute and report problems\n\nSee [CONTRIBUTING](CONTRIBUTING.md) for the workflow and [SECURITY](SECURITY.md) for private vulnerability reporting. A useful rendering issue includes engine/RHI, resolution, preset, quality tier and an isolated reproduction.\n\n## License\n\n**GPL-2.0-or-later**, with third-party notices and the Blinker font's separate OFL terms. [L2]   "content": "# lever\n\n**Feedback loops for coding agents.** A Copilot plugin.\n\n![/lever <verb> <your words>: the verb picks the playbook, the rest is you talking normally](docs/examples/try.png)\n\n```bash\ncopilot plugin marketplace add github/lever\ncopilot plugin install lever@lever\n```\n\nIn the Copilot app, open these links. Each one asks you to confirm, then opens a pre-filled form:\n\n1. [Add the marketplace](ghapp://plugins/marketplace/add?source=github%2Flever) (`github/lever`)\n2. [Install the plugin](ghapp://plugins/install?source=lever%40lever) (`lever@lever`)\n\nOr do it by hand: **Customize → + Add → Marketplace** with `github/lever`, then **+ Add → Plugin** with `lever@lever`.\n\nStart a new session and try one that only reads:\n\n```text\n/lever loop our test suite feels slow. just the card, don't change anything\n```\n\nYou get a Loop Card back: the metric, how to measure it, how noisy it is, and what counts as a win. Nothing gets pushed, filed or merged.\n\n## Why\n\nAgents get really good once they can check their own work. Give one a number, a way to measure it and a bar for \"better\", and it'll grind on that for hours without you. Without that, you're the loop: pasting screenshots, eyeballing scroll jank, hitting rerun on CI at midnight.\n\nSetting up the loop is the hard part. What do you measure? How noisy is it? What's a real win and what's a lucky run? When do you stop? Most people skip it, which is fair, because it's annoying. lever asks you those questions, writes the answers down, and then lets agents iterate against it.\n\nIt comes from how some of the most AI-forward engineers at GitHub work day to day: CI speedups, a five-day crate split run from three terminals, weeks of [unattended delivery](https://gist.github.com/EvanBoyle/8c1a97f682d92dab8c09d0e1ea73f4a0), and the automations that took over the chores. We mined our own sessions for what kept working, then put most of the effort into making it one command. Same workflow, no PhD required.\n\n## What it looks like\n\n![/lever routes a plain-words ask to the right verb](docs/examples/lever.png)\n\n![/lever loop turns \"it feels slow\" into a Loop Card](docs/examples/loop.png)\n\n![/lever autonomy shows and sets your dial](docs/examples/autonomy.png)\n\nMore in the **[examples gallery](docs/examples.md)**: experiment arms, a brief, the three-terminal refactor, the PR shepherd, cross-model review, an automation, and the verbs that tune lever to you.\n\n<details><summary>Copy-pasteable examples</summary>\n\n```text\n/lever our CI is slow and I'm tired of hitting rerun\n/lever loop the editor feels janky when I scroll big files\n/lever arms try the 6 ideas on the card\n/lever brief add offline mode to the editor. ship it by tomorrow\n/lever refactor src/core is 400k lines. cut it in half\n/lever shepherd keep my stack green till it lands\n/lever review this PR\n/lever automate make the stack shepherd an automation for this repo\n/lever mirror last 30 days\n/lever steer push immediately, then verify\n/lever autonomy agents can merge docs PRs in this repo, nothing else\n```\n\n</details>\n\n## Commands\n\n```text\n/lever <what's bugging you>      not sure? describe it. lever picks the verb.\n\nBUILD   make something new\n  brief <ask>                    turn ~20 words into a brief an agent can run unattended\n  deliver [brief|issues]         run lanes in parallel and land the work\n  refactor <scope> <goal>        huge mechanical change: producer, packager, shepherd\n  backlog                        keep enough ready issues in the pool\n  shepherd [pr|stack]            keep PRs green until they land\n  land [prs]                     merge plan for a stack or a batch\n  status                         progress you never have to ask for\n\nLOOP    make something measurably better\n  loop <problem>                 find the feedback loop first: a Loop Card\n  arms [ideas]                   one agent per idea, against a control\n  review [pr|plan]               several models, blind; only agreed findings\n\nRUN     make it happen without you\n  automate <task>                turn a chore into a paused Copilot Automation\n  health                         why did it stall? one fix, or \"no change\"\n\nYOU     tune lever to how you work\n  mirror [30d]                   a scorecard of how you prompt, from your sessions\n  steer <correction>             say it once, never again\n  autonomy [L0-L5|<words>]       who merges. see or set your dial\n  spend [standard|high|max]      how much model to throw at it\n  setup                          first run: set your dials\n  help [verb]                    this list, or one verb in detail\n```\n\nEach verb is a skill in [`skills/`](skills/). The `/` menu shows only `/lever`. Skills that only read and advise, like `loop`, can still load on their own when your ask fits. Anything that pushes, files, opens PRs or schedules runs waits for `/lever <verb>` or an explicit ask.\n\n## Your dials\n\n- **[Autonomy](docs/autonomy.md)**, L0 to L5: who merges. L0 only proposes. L2 gets PRs green and you merge. L5 lands, releases and watches. It's your setting, saved in `~/.copilot/lever.yml`, and your repo's branch protection still wins. Start at L2 and turn it up as you trust it.\n- **[Spend](docs/spend.md)**, `standard` · `high` · `max`: model tier, parallel lanes, review depth and how often things run. A repo can cap it in `.github/lever.yml`.\n\n`/lever setup` asks three questions and writes both ([example](config/personal.example.yml)). For a team, copy [`config/autonomy.example.yml`](config/autonomy.example.yml) to `.github/lever.yml`.\n\nWork lever starts is tracked as an issue assigned to you with the [`lever` label](docs/tracking.md), so `/lever status` can list everything in flight, needs-you first.\n\n## Other ways to install\n\n**Per repo**, so the Copilot coding agent in the cloud gets the skills too:\n\n```bash\nmkdir -p .github/skills\ncp -r path/to/lever/skills/* .github/skills/\ncp -r path/to/lever/{docs,templates,config,automations} .github/\n```\n\nSkills link to `../../docs/...`, so those four folders have to sit next to `skills/`.\n\n**Hacking on lever:** clone it and run `copilot plugin marketplace add ./lever`, then `copilot plugin install lever@lever`. It loads straight from your checkout, so edits show up in your next session.\n\n**Automations:** the recipes in [`automations/`](automations/) install through the GitHub MCP server with `/lever automate`. Each one starts paused, dry-runs on past events, and only then gets turned on. The Copilot app has the automation tools built in; in Copilot CLI, start with `copilot --enable-all-github-mcp-tools`.\n\n## Make it yours\n\nThese skills fit how we work. Yours will be different. `/lever mirror` reads your own session history and shows you what you keep repeating, and `/lever steer` turns those repeated corrections into rules that stick. Fork it and bend it.\n\n## Status\n\nEarly. Issues and PRs welcome.\n\n## License\n\nMIT. See [LICENSE](LICENSE).\n",

[L2]   "content": "# ub-mode\n\n`ub-mode` is an agent skill that enforces disciplined software engineering principles when writing or changing code. It is loosely based on portions of [@poteto](https://github.com/poteto)'s rules (`poteto-mode` / `pstack`), reduced and paired with deterministic quality-gate tools:\n\n1. **First Make it Work** — Laziness Protocol, Foundational Thinking, TDD, Redesign From First Principles, Attack the Premise, Subtract Before You Add, Outcome-Oriented Execution, Build the Lever, and Architecture (Model the Domain, Boundary Discipline, Type System Discipline, Make Operations Idempotent, Separate Before Serializing Shared State).\n2. **Then Make it Right** — Fix Root Causes, Sequence Work into Verifiable Units, Test Behavior (Not Implementation), [Crapper](https://github.com/unclebob/crapper) (`CRAP < 10`), [Dryer](https://github.com/unclebob/dryer) (duplication `< 0.8`), [Mutator](https://github.com/unclebob/mutator) (cover the uncovered, kill the survivors, delete dead code), and Refactoring.\n3. **Practice** — Keep a Log, Guard the Context Window, Worktree Cleanup, and Commit and Push in small ordered commits.\n\n## Companion Tool Repositories\n\n`ub-mode` relies on deterministic quality-gate tools to enforce structure, complexity, duplication, and test thoroughness:\n\n- [unclebob/crapper](https://github.com/unclebob/crapper) — Computes cyclomatic complexity, test coverage, and CRAP score per function so every function stays under the CRAP threshold (`< 10`).\n- [unclebob/dryer](https://github.com/unclebob/dryer) — Detects structural code duplication so duplicate blocks (`>= 0.8` similarity) are eliminated.\n- [unclebob/mutator](https://github.com/unclebob/mutator) — Runs mutation testing to expose uncovered code and surviving mutants that tests fail to catch.\n- [unclebob/uml-viewer](https://github.com/unclebob/uml-viewer) — Visualizes components, coverage, CRAP, mutation scores, and dependency directions.\n\n## Installation\n\nCopy `SKILL.md` into your agent's skills directory as `ub-mode/SKILL.md` (for example `~/.grok/skills/ub-mode/SKILL.md`, `~/.claude/skills/ub-mode/SKILL.md`, or `~/.cursor/skills/ub-mode/SKILL.md`), then invoke `/ub-mode`.\n",

[L2]   "content": "<div align=\"center\">\n\n<img src=\"https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SoMarkAI/image_bed/main/OXR_README/assets/header.png\" alt=\"\" />\n\n<h1>SoMark｜O<span style=\"color: #DE7802;\">X</span>R</h1>\n\nAn open-source document parsing model with SOTA accuracy and speed, using an RSI loop during post-training.\n\n---\n\n**Turn documents into Agent-Friendly data.**\n\n[🌐 Online Demo](https://free-oxr.somark.ai) ｜ [🔥 🆓 Free API](#free-api)\n\n[![GitHub | OXR](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-OXR-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github)](https://github.com/SoMarkAI/OXR)   [![Hugging Face | OXR-1.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/Hugging%20Face-OXR--1.0-F59E0B?style=flat-square)](https://huggingface.co/SoMarkAI/OXR-1.0)   [![ModelScope | OXR-1.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/ModelScope-OXR--1.0-624AFF?style=flat-square)](https://modelscope.cn/models/SoMark/OXR-1.0)\n![arXiv | Coming Soon](https://img.shields.io/badge/arXiv-Coming%20Soon-B31B1B?style=flat-square)\n\n**English** · [简体中文](README_CN.md)\n\n</div>\n\nOXR (Optical Everything Recognition) is an open-source model from the SoMark team. It turns PDFs and document images into Agent-Friendly data in Markdown or JSON, with layout coordinates included.\n\nPretrained from scratch, OXR uses a recursive self-improvement (RSI) loop during post-training—a first in document parsing. With just 1.3B parameters, OXR ranks #1 on olmOCR-Bench, OmniDocBench, and DocParsingBench while delivering industry-leading parsing speed.\n\nOXR is the first to make its layout analysis module independent and pluggable. This design accelerates parsing and supports replacing the built-in layout model with a custom one. OXR continues to handle content recognition and reading order, enabling adaptation across diverse scenarios with minimal integration effort.\n\n![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SoMarkAI/image_bed/main/OXR_README/assets/three-benchmark-leaderboards-olm-main.png)\n\n![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SoMarkAI/image_bed/main/OXR_README/assets/speed-score-overview.png)\n\n---\n\n> If this project helps you, please click ⭐ Star in the top-right corner to support us. It's the best encouragement you can give the developers!\n\n\n\n## Why OXR?\n\n- 🎯 SOTA Accuracy. #1 Across Three Benchmarks.\n\n  - OXR ranks 🏆#1 on olmOCR-Bench, OmniDocBench, and DocParsingBench, with a particularly wide lead in table parsing.\n  - OXR can recognize 13 document element types, from formulas and tables to chemical equations, chemical structures, and code blocks, with bounding box coordinates included. It also performs well on challenging documents and layouts, including A3 exam papers, newspapers, vertical text, and handwriting.\n  - See [docs/benchmark.md](docs/benchmark.md) for the full results and instructions to reproduce the evaluations.\n- 🚀 1.3B Parameters. Top-Tier Parsing Speed.\n\n  - With only 1.3B parameters, OXR ranks 🏆#1 among open-source document parsing models in speed tests on the RTX PRO 6000.\n  - OXR redesign its processing architecture at the task level to improve parsing speed while maintaining accuracy.\n  - See [docs/benchmark.md](docs/benchmark.md) for the full results and instructions to reproduce the evaluations.\n- 🧩 Pluggable Layout Analysis. Document Structure on Your Terms.\n\n  - Layout analysis requirements vary widely across domains. Even for the same document, element types, region boundaries, and grouping rules can differ depending on the business use case.\n  - OXR is the first to make layout analysis independent and pluggable. Its built-in layout model can be replaced while retaining OXR’s recognition and reading order capabilities, enabling adaptation across document scenarios with minimal integration effort.\n  - See the [How it works](#how-to-works) section below for details.\n\n\n<details>\n<summary>Expand to see all 13 element types</summary>\n\n| Name | JSON type value | Content or output format |\n|-|-|-|\n| Caption | Caption | Plain text |\n| Footnote | Footnote | Plain text |\n| Formula | Formula | LaTeX |\n| Text | Text | Plain text |\n| Footer | Page-footer | Plain text (filtered out by default) |\n| Header | Page-header | Plain text (filtered out by default) |\n| Figure | Picture | Image |\n| Title | Title | Plain text |\n| Table | Table | HTML / Markdown |\n| Stamp | Stamp | Plain text / Image |\n| Chemical Equation | Chemical Equation | LaTeX (starting with \\ce, using mhchem syntax) |\n| Code Block | Code Block | Markdown code block |\n| Chemical Structure | Chemical Structure | SMILES / Image |\n\n\n</details>\n\n\n## Parsing Examples\n\nThe animation shows OXR's parsing process.\n\n![Animated OXR parsing example](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SoMarkAI/image_bed/main/OXR_README/assets/oxr_parsing_demo.gif)\n\nThe examples below show OXR parsing different document types.
